acceptance: all 16 episodes write a `pairs_run.json` naming `planner: deepseek`, `policy: null` and the model config
the `full` arm's reader episodes file non-empty `memory_retrieval` records; the `wo_episodic_memory` arm files none and passes `Ablation.violations()`
MEM-1's `episodic_memory_MEM_1.json` carries the seat fields and the model-seat `seat_note`
the batch's two-ledger spend is reported, with `http_requests` (made) and `http_requests_successful` (returned) side by side
artefact_rule: not /tmp, not a single point: each pair-arm keeps its own store and episodes, and the three JSON summaries beside the run are the source lines

cost.measured_from: E1's own `em_*` batch ledgers, read with `batch_spend` (the two-ledger reader added in P6-a): the same case family, the same seat, the same config, so this is a measurement of the same thing rather than a guess

share_of_requests_that_returned_nothing.note: E1 spent 707 of 3,292 requests this way, all 429s after retries plus 17 schema errors. It is why the bound comes from the worst cell: a mean is computed mostly over cells that escaped the limiter.

cost.stop_rule: halt before the 17th episode if the batch's two-ledger `http_requests` reaches 411; on a halt, report what ran and what did not, and do not resume into the same directory (the store beside it is append-only)
cost.upper_bound_arithmetic: worst cell 17.13 req/ep x 16 episodes x 1.5 = 411; the margin covers a batch that meets the limiter harder than any E1 cell did, which SPEC §11's risk register lists as outside this project's control
cost.why_requests_not_usd: the endpoint is free and no price is configured, so a money figure would be invented; the request is also the unit the provider's rate limiter is denominated in, and on E1 that limiter — not the token count — decided what the batch got

credentials: never recorded; a config names the env var, not the key (SPEC 7)

decided_by.D1: the text seat is `configs/models/bst_text_agnes.yaml` — the same one E1 ran, so this batch's ledgers are comparable with E1's rather than being a second seat
decided_by.D2: bound declared here at 411 requests, measured from E1 and set from its worst cell, before the first request of this batch
decided_by.D5: road A — this closes the one §13.2 row v0.3 could not close, and it is the cheapest of the three outstanding gaps

experiment: MEM-1 on a model decision source — §11's Memory group, which had no reading on one (SPEC §11 Memory, §13.2 row 2)

identity.note: written after the commit that added the seat, so the tree is dirty by exactly this file; it is committed next, and the batch runs from a clean tree

product_change_this_batch_depends_on.contract: tests/contract/test_v03_episodic_seat.py (20 checks) with 12/12 mutations verified to bite (work/v03/p6b_mutation_check.py)
product_change_this_batch_depends_on.what: `em-pairs` gained `--planner`/`--model-config`; `run_episodic_pairs` derives the policy from the seat; MEM-1 carries the seat into its artefact
product_change_this_batch_depends_on.zero_spend_rehearsal: the rule seat ran end to end first — 4 pairs x 2 arms = 16 episodes over 8 stores, `offline: true`, giving the baseline this batch is read against

seat.same_seat_as: E1 (identical config), so the two batches' ledgers are comparable
seat.store_and_ablation_kept: the experience store and the arm's ablation both stay on, which is the object of the measurement
seat.why_policy_is_none: `MemoryPolicy` answers from `ctx.model_payload()` and is itself a decision maker; `run_group` refuses `policy="memory"` beside a model planner precisely because two decision makers make a row's source unnameable. `run_episodic_pairs` derives the policy from the seat, so the incoherent batch cannot be expressed.

shape.episodes_arithmetic: 4 pairs x 2 arms x 2 roles = 16 episodes, one store per pair-arm
shape.pairs_are: the frozen set's own four (EM_PAIRS); `--pairs` is not narrowed
shape.why_privileged: the Memory group's question is whether the reader uses what the writer left. Rendering a camera would add a second, unmeasured difference between the arms, so perception is held fixed and the reader is the only thing that varies.

the_confound_stated_up_front.consequence: a within-pair trajectory difference is NOT attributable to memory alone, and this table is not comparable with a rule-seat table as if it were the same experiment
the_confound_stated_up_front.recorded_in_the_artefact: `planner`, `policy`, `model_config` and a `seat_note` are in `pairs_run.json`, `pairs_measured.json` AND `episodic_memory_MEM_1.json`, so a reader of the published table cannot mistake the two seats
the_confound_stated_up_front.what: on a model seat the two arms differ in memory AND in the draw
what_it_does_not_establish: that a model reader uses memory *more* than a rule reader — the two seats differ in far more than memory, so no such comparison is licensed
any rate: n=4 pairs is an existence proof for the instruments, not a sample (the same `unit_note` MEM-1 already carries on the rule seat)
the_confound_stated_up_front.why: a model planner is stochastic; the rule seat's reader is a deterministic policy, so there the arms differ only in memory

why_this_batch_exists: §11's Memory group (M1–M4) is defined by MEM-1 over the episodic **pair** protocol: a writer episode leaves residue, a reader episode queries it, and the two arms differ in whether retrieval happens.

That protocol's only entry point hard-coded `planner_kind="rule"`, so every M1–M4 reading this project has is a rule-policy reading. On a model decision source the group had **no** reading — a structural gap, not a measurement that was skipped, and the reason v0.3's §13.2 row 2 reads 'partially met'.
P6-b added the seat. This batch is what runs on it.
written_by: work/v03/p6c_write_prereg.py (no number in this file is hand-typed: the per-episode cost, the projection and the bound are all read off E1's ledgers with batch_spend)
